b: Justification is a courtroom word. Adoption is a family word. It says that the person who was a rebel and a stranger is now welcomed as a child into the house. The Bible uses both pictures, and the two together are a fuller account of the gospel than either alone.

In the Roman world an adopted son received the name, the family and the inheritance of his new father, with full legal standing, and often chosen over natural born sons. Paul draws on that. He says that God sent his Son "to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5). Those who believe have "received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (Romans 8:15).

The effects are immediate. A child has a new relationship, a new name and a new access. We may speak to God as Father, as Jesus taught. A child also has a new security: "The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children. And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ" (Romans 8:16-17). Everything that belongs to Christ is shared with those who are in him. And a child has a family. Adopted people are brothers and sisters, and the church is the household of God.

John's wonder at this is plain. "Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are!" (1 John 3:1). He adds that we do not yet know what we will be, but we know that when Christ appears, we will be like him.

The adoption of believers is not a legal fiction. It is a real change of status and relationship, accomplished by God at great cost, and its goal is that those who were far off may be at home with him.
adopted-into-the-family.q: What changes if you believe that God relates to you as a child and not as a servant or a stranger?

b: The Bible takes for granted that the visible world is not all there is. It speaks of a great number of spiritual beings, called angels, and also of a rebellion among them. The teaching is smaller and more modest than much popular imagination, but it is real, and it matters for how Christians think about spiritual life.

Angels are created beings. They are not divine, and they are not former humans. Paul says that thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities were all created through Christ and for him (Colossians 1:16). Hebrews describes them as "ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation" (Hebrews 1:14). They worship God (Isaiah 6), carry messages (Luke 1), protect (Psalm 91:11) and carry out his judgments. Names are rare. Only Michael and Gabriel are named in the sixty-six books. When people try to worship an angel in Scripture, the angel stops them (Revelation 22:8-9).

The Bible also speaks of Satan, the adversary, and of demons. Most Christians have read Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 as describing the fall of a created being through pride, though many scholars say that these chapters are first about earthly kings. The New Testament says that the devil "has been sinning from the very start," and that Jesus came "to destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8). He is powerful but limited. He is a liar and a tempter, a "roaring lion" looking for someone to devour, but believers are told to resist him and he will flee (1 Peter 5:8; James 4:7).

Christians differ about how far to speak of demonic activity in daily life, and about whether each person has a guardian angel. The sober center is that angels serve God and his people, that the devil is a defeated enemy, and that Christ has triumphed over every power by his cross (Colossians 2:15).

Baptism is the rite of washing with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, by which a person is welcomed into the Christian community. Jesus commanded it in the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19), and Christians have practiced it from the very first. On Pentecost Peter told the crowd to "Repent and be baptized," and about three thousand were baptized that day (Acts 2:38,41).

The Bible gives several meanings to it. It is a sign of washing and cleansing from sin. It is a picture of union with Christ in his death and resurrection: "We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). It is a mark of belonging to the people of God, and it is the public sign of faith.

Christians disagree on three questions. The first is who should be baptized. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian and many other churches baptize infants, seeing a parallel with circumcision and the household baptisms in Acts, and holding that baptism marks entry into the covenant community. Baptist, Pentecostal and many other churches baptize only those who profess faith, arguing that the New Testament examples show belief preceding baptism. Both have defenders from the early church.

The second is the mode. The Greek word baptizo means to dip or immerse, and many churches immerse. Others pour or sprinkle. An early church manual, the Didache, written perhaps around AD 100, allows pouring water three times on the head when there is not enough for immersion. The third question is what baptism does. Some traditions say it conveys regeneration. Others say it is a sign of what God has already done. A small number, such as the Quakers, do not practice water baptism.

Nearly all Christian traditions agree that baptism is not optional and that its meaning is union with Christ, and most recognize each other's baptisms if they were done with water in the name of the Trinity.

Justification declares a person right with God once for all. Sanctification is the lifelong process in which that person is made holy. The word means to be set apart, and it covers both a position and a growth. In one sense, believers are already sanctified, set apart for God by Christ. In another sense, they are being sanctified, becoming in practice what they already are in standing.

Paul gives the aim bluntly: "It is God's will that you should be holy" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). He also describes how it works, with both halves of the truth in one sentence. "continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose" (Philippians 2:12-13). Believers must make an effort, and the effort is empowered by God. In another passage he says that "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).

The means are ordinary. They include prayer, the reading and hearing of Scripture, worship, the Lord's Supper, fellowship with other believers, service, and the discipline of obedience. They are called means of grace, because God uses them to give what he promises. Suffering is another, since Peter says that trials refine faith as fire refines gold.

Traditions differ on how far sanctification goes in this life. The Reformed tradition teaches progressive sanctification: a real growth that is never completed before death, and in which the struggle with sin continues. John Wesley taught that Christians could aim at "entire sanctification" or "Christian perfection," which he defined as a heart filled with love for God and neighbor, not a state free from mistakes. Others, in the Keswick tradition, taught a decisive "higher life" of surrender. The Orthodox Church speaks of a journey of theosis. John writes plainly that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8), and that everyone with the hope of seeing Christ purifies himself.

The Bible says that human beings are made of more than one part, but it does not give a single neat answer on how many. Genesis describes the first man as dust shaped by God and filled with breath, becoming a living creature. He is body and breath, and he is one person.

Over the centuries Christians have used three main frameworks. Dichotomy holds that a person has two parts, a material body and an immaterial soul, or spirit, with the two words describing the same inner part. Jesus seems to say this when he tells his hearers not to fear those who "kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28). Trichotomy holds that there are three parts, body, soul and spirit, and points to Paul's prayer that "your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless" (1 Thessalonians 5:23), and to Hebrews 4:12. Holism, which has grown in popularity, says that the Bible views the person as an integrated unity, and that words such as soul, spirit and heart describe aspects of the whole person rather than separate parts.

The question has practical effects. If a person is a body-soul unit, then the body matters, and the Christian hope is not an escape from the body but its redemption. That is why the Bible does not speak of floating souls as the final goal. Paul says that "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable" and that it is "raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). The Apostles' Creed says, "I believe in the resurrection of the body."

Another matter is what happens between death and resurrection. Most Christians hold that the soul survives death and is with the Lord, as Paul suggests when he says he would "prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). A few hold that the person sleeps until the resurrection. The next lessons on last things return to this.

Does a Christian ever fall away? The question has a pastoral side: how can someone be sure of salvation? And a doctrinal side: what is the relationship between God's grace and human faithfulness? The Bible has comforting promises and also solemn warnings, and Christians have held different views of how they fit together.

The promises are strong. Jesus says of his sheep, "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand" (John 10:28). Paul asks who can separate us from the love of Christ and concludes that "neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). John says that he writes "so that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13).

The warnings are strong as well. Hebrews speaks of those who have been enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift and have fallen away, and it says that it is impossible to restore them again to repentance (Hebrews 6:4-6). Jesus tells his disciples to remain in him.

Reformed and Baptist traditions teach the perseverance of the saints: those whom God has truly saved will be kept by him to the end, and those who fall away show that their faith was not real. This is sometimes loosely called "once saved, always saved," though the phrase suggests that a decision is enough without a changed life. Arminian and Wesleyan traditions teach that believers are secure in Christ but may through persistent unbelief or deliberate sin forsake the faith. Catholic teaching holds that grace can be lost by mortal sin and restored by confession. Orthodox teaching speaks of an ongoing journey, with real dangers.

On one thing all agree: the believer's security rests on Christ's faithfulness and not on his own grip. And the Bible expects those who belong to Christ to know it, through the Spirit, through the fruit of a changed life, and through the promises of the gospel.
can-you-lose-it-perseverance-and-assuran.q: What gives you assurance that you belong to Christ, and what threatens it?

b: Few teachings have caused more argument among Christians than election and predestination, though the words are the Bible's own. Paul writes that God "chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:4-5). Romans 8 lays out a chain: those God foreknew, he predestined, called, justified and glorified.

The disagreement is about the basis of God's choice. One view, held by Augustine, Luther, Calvin and the Reformed tradition, says God's election is unconditional. He chose particular people for salvation purely out of his own mercy, not because of anything he foresaw in them, and his grace to them is effective. In the early seventeenth century a Dutch pastor named Jacobus Arminius questioned this, and after his death his followers presented their view, which was condemned at the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619. The Synod's answer, in five points, is where the five points of Calvinism come from, which later generations remembered by the acronym TULIP.

The other main view, held by Arminians and Wesleyans, says that God elects on the basis of foreknowledge of who will believe, or that election is corporate, belonging to the people of God in Christ, and that individuals enter by faith. They point to the verse saying that God our Savior "wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:3-4) and to the statement that God is "not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance" (2 Peter 3:9).

Catholic and Orthodox traditions, while differing from each other, generally hold that God's grace is first and necessary but that people cooperate with it. Reformed readers answer that a human cooperation that decides the matter would make salvation depend on us after all.

Whatever one decides, the text's own aim is not to alarm but to comfort and to produce praise. Paul begins with a blessing: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Jesus offers a promise that every believer can rest in: "the one who comes to Me I will never drive away" (John 6:37).

The Bible begins with the statement that God created the heavens and the earth, and it never wavers from it. Christians have drawn from the text a doctrine called creation out of nothing, or in Latin creatio ex nihilo. It says that God did not make the world out of pre-existing matter, and that nothing existed alongside him. He called everything into being.

The key verses are brief. "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth," says the psalm. "For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm" (Psalm 33:6,9). The writer of Hebrews says that "the universe was formed at God's command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible" (Hebrews 11:3). Paul says all things in heaven and on earth were created through Christ and for him.

The doctrine matters for several reasons. It says that God is distinct from his creation. The world is not a part of God, and it is not a rival to him. It says that matter is good, since God made it from nothing and called it good. It also means the world depends on God for its existence at every moment, not just at the beginning.

Christians differ over how to read the details of Genesis 1 and the age of the earth. Young earth creationists read the six days as ordinary days a few thousand years ago. Old earth creationists accept the scientific dating of the universe at some 13.8 billion years and read the days as ages or as a literary framework. Some accept the evidence for biological evolution and see it as the method God used, while others reject it. These are serious debates, but they are debates among people who agree that God made all there is, and that it is good.

What happens to a person at death, before the resurrection and the final judgment? The Bible says less than we might like, and Christians have held a few views. It does give clear promises to believers. Jesus told the thief on the cross, "Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Paul writes to the Philippians that he is torn between living and dying: "I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed" (Philippians 1:23). And to the Corinthians: he would "prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8).

The view of most Christians, called the intermediate state, is that the souls of believers go at once into the presence of Christ and wait there for the resurrection of the body. It is a state of joy, but not the final one, since the person is not yet whole. A minority of Christians, including some Adventists, hold that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, a view often called soul sleep, and they note that Scripture often calls death sleep.

The Catholic Church teaches that those who die in grace but still need to be cleansed from the effects of sin pass through purgatory before entering heaven. Protestants reject that teaching, holding that Christ's work is complete and that the Bible does not teach a place of purification. The Orthodox churches pray for the dead but do not hold a fully developed doctrine of purgatory.

The Bible treats death as an enemy. Paul calls it "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Hebrews says that people are destined to die once and after that to face judgment. But because Christ has died and risen, believers do not face it alone, and Paul can say, "to live is Christ, and to die is gain." The comfort of the gospel is not that death is nothing, but that it is no longer the last word.

When Jesus began to preach, he said two things: "Repent and believe in the gospel!" (Mark 1:15). Paul later summed up his own message as "repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ" (Acts 20:21). They are two sides of one turning.

Repentance means a change of mind that leads to a change of direction. The Greek word, metanoia, means to think differently afterward. It includes knowing that one has sinned, feeling sorrow over it, and turning away from it toward God. Paul distinguishes two kinds of sorrow: "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). The difference is that godly sorrow turns toward God, while worldly sorrow only turns inward in regret or fear of punishment.

Faith is trust. The Bible does not mean by it a vague optimism or a belief in something with no evidence. Hebrews says, "Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see" (Hebrews 11:1). Theologians divide faith into three parts. It involves knowledge, because we must know the message. It involves assent, agreement that it is true. And it involves trust, resting on Christ personally to save us. The last is the heart of it. A person can believe that a bridge is sound and still not walk across it.

Faith is also not a work that earns salvation. It is the empty hand that receives the gift. Paul says that salvation is by grace "through faith," and "this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God." Even the faith is a gift. Christians differ over how far it is a gift given directly by God to the chosen and how far it is given to all who hear, but in both views the praise goes to God.
Repentance and faith are not one-time events only. They mark the whole Christian life, since a believer goes on turning from sin and trusting Christ daily.
faith-and-repentance.q: What does repentance look like in your life this week: a turn, a confession, or a decision to do something differently?

b: Many readers meet a puzzle when they set two statements side by side. Paul says that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28). James says that a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone (James 2:24). Martin Luther, in his preface to the New Testament in 1522, called James "an epistle of straw," though he later softened his view. Are the two in conflict?

Most Christian interpreters say no, and the reason is in the words. Paul is dealing with a particular question: how can a sinner be put right with God? His answer is that the basis is not the works of the law, meaning the observances that marked out Israel, such as circumcision, but faith in Christ. James is dealing with a different question: how do you know a profession of faith is genuine? His answer is that real faith produces action. He says, "faith without deeds is dead" (James 2:26), and gives the examples of Abraham and Rahab.

The two also use the words in different senses. Paul uses "justify" to mean a declaration that someone is righteous in God's sight. James is using it in a way that means a faith is shown to be true, vindicated by what it does. They also use "faith" differently. For James, a faith that is merely agreeing to facts, which "even the demons believe" (James 2:19), is not real faith at all.

Paul himself insists on the same thing. In the same chapter of Ephesians that says we are saved by grace, through faith, and not by works, he goes on to say, "For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works" (Ephesians 2:10). In Galatians he says that what matters is "faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6).
A short summary is that we are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone. It is the root, and works are the fruit.

Romans 8 gives a chain of five links that stretches from before time to after it: "those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified" (Romans 8:30). The last link is stated in the past tense, as if it were already done, because for those who belong to Christ the outcome is certain.

Glorification means that believers will be completely freed from sin and its effects, and will share in the glory of Christ. It will take place when he returns. John says, "we know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2). Paul says that the Lord Jesus Christ "will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body" (Philippians 3:21).

Glorification has several parts. The soul will be made perfect, with no remaining sin or longing for it. The body will be raised, no longer subject to decay, weakness and death. Paul says, "we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed, in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:51-52). The creation will be renewed, so that the whole world is set free. And the people of God will live in his presence forever.

This is the final answer to the problem set out in the earlier lessons of this course. The fall damaged the whole of humanity, and the cross and resurrection begin the healing, and glorification completes it. Christians are not told to expect a perfect life now, but to hold on with hope. "Our citizenship is in heaven," Paul says, and "we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ" (Philippians 3:20).

The Bible claims to be more than a record of human religious ideas. Paul puts it in one memorable sentence: "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16). The word translated God-breathed, in Greek theopneustos, is unique in the New Testament. It does not say that God breathed into the writers. It says the writings themselves are breathed out by him.

Peter says how it worked: "no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21). The human authors were not secretaries taking dictation. They wrote in their own styles, from their own settings, using their own research (Luke 1:1-4) and memories. Yet the result is also God's word. Christians call this inspiration, and the shape of it is often compared to the person of Christ, who is fully human and fully divine.

Jesus treats the Old Testament as authoritative. He says that not a letter or stroke of the Law will pass away until everything is fulfilled (Matthew 5:18), he settles arguments by saying "it is written," and he says that Scripture cannot be set aside (John 10:35). The apostles treat each other's writings as Scripture too. Peter refers to Paul's letters among "the other Scriptures" (2 Peter 3:16).

Because it is inspired, the Bible is authoritative. It is the standard by which the church tests its teaching, its worship and its life. Christians differ on how to describe that authority in detail, and the next lesson looks at some of the words they use. But the basic claim is shared across the church: that when Scripture speaks, God speaks.

Two statements in the Bible seem to some readers to pull in opposite directions. John says, "God is love" (1 John 4:8). And the same God, in the passage where he describes himself to Moses, says that he forgives iniquity, transgression and sin, "yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" (Exodus 34:7). How can both be true?

The answer begins with seeing that love, in the Bible, is not mere sentiment. It is a firm commitment to the good of another, and it takes sin seriously because sin damages the one loved. A parent who did not care how a child was treated would not be loving. A judge who let a violent person go free would not be kind, but would be failing the victims. God's justice is part of his love. It is his love for the world, set against whatever destroys it.

The great question then is how God can forgive sinners and still be just. Paul says that the cross is where the two meet. God presented Jesus "as an atoning sacrifice in His blood through faith, in order to demonstrate His righteousness," so as "to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:25-26). Justice is satisfied, and mercy is offered, in one act.

The love of God is shown in the Bible at its fullest in the gift of the Son: "This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him" (1 John 4:9). Love does not mean that God overlooks sin. It means that he paid the price himself, and an honest reading of Scripture will not drop either truth in favor of the other.

If one word sums up the Christian message, it is grace. In the New Testament the Greek word is charis, a word that in ordinary use meant a favor, a gift or a kindness. Paul bends it to a special use: the free, undeserved kindness of God toward people who deserve the opposite.

The classic statement is in Ephesians 2. After describing human beings as dead in sin, Paul says, "But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved!" (Ephesians 2:4-5). A few verses later: "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Three things stand out. First, grace is undeserved. It is not given because of any merit, and it cannot be earned. If it could, Paul says, "grace would no longer be grace" (Romans 11:6). Second, grace is free and it is costly. It costs the receiver nothing, but it cost the giver everything, since forgiveness was paid for on the cross. Third, grace is not only about forgiveness. It is also the power that changes people. Titus says that "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions" (Titus 2:11-12).

Christian traditions have different ways of describing how grace works. Some distinguish prevenient grace, which comes before we respond, saving grace, and sustaining grace. Catholic theology speaks of grace as a gift that can be channeled through the sacraments. Reformed theology stresses that grace is sovereign. But all insist that it is the foundation of everything, and that the proper response is gratitude.
grace.q: Where in your own life are you still trying to earn what God has said he gives freely?

b: The death of Jesus is not the end of his story. On the third day he rose from the dead, in a real body that could be touched and that ate fish, but that also passed through closed doors. The resurrection was not a resuscitation, like that of Lazarus, who would die again. It was a new kind of bodily life, the beginning of the new creation. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits, the first piece of a harvest still to come.

Forty days later, according to Luke, he ascended into heaven. The disciples watched him taken up in a cloud, and two men in white said, "This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11). The ascension is not just a farewell. It is the enthronement of the king. Christ now sits at the right hand of the Father, a place of honor and authority.

What is he doing there? The New Testament says first that he rules. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him. Second, he intercedes for his people. Hebrews says, "Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them" (Hebrews 7:25). Third, he prepares a place for his followers, and sends the Spirit. And fourth, he waits, until his enemies are put under his feet.

Most Christians confess that Christ will return visibly. That is the subject of a lesson on last things. For now it is enough to notice what the resurrection and ascension together mean. The one who suffered is now Lord of all, and the life of the believer is hidden with him there, which is why Paul says, "set your minds on things above" (Colossians 3:2).

Popular pictures of heaven often draw more from cartoons than from Scripture, with people floating on clouds and playing harps. The Bible's picture is richer. In its widest sense, heaven is the place where God dwells, and the believer's destination is to be with him. Jesus says, "In My Father’s house are many rooms," and he is going there "to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). Paul says that to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and the dying thief was promised Paradise.

But the final hope is not just a spirit-world far away. The last chapters of the Bible say that the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven to a new earth, and that "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Revelation 21:3). The goal is the renewal of creation, and God's coming to live in it. Isaiah's vision of new heavens and a new earth includes houses built and lived in, vineyards planted and eaten from, and wolf and lamb feeding together. Paul says that "the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God" (Romans 8:21).

The best-known details are about what will not be there: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain." And the best is about what will be: "they will see His face." The great blessing is the presence of God, and everything else, such as friendship, rest, work, worship and beauty, flows from it.

The Bible is modest about the rest. We are told that there will be rewards and varied responsibilities, that the nations will bring their glory into the city, and that the saints will reign. The writers do not try to describe everything. They tell us enough to want it and to trust the one who has prepared it.
heaven.q: What do you most look forward to about the new creation, and does it change anything about today?

b: Of all the Bible's teachings, hell is the hardest to hear, and a faithful account must say that it comes mostly from the lips of Jesus. He speaks of it more than anyone else in the New Testament, using the image of Gehenna, a valley outside Jerusalem associated with fire and refuse, and speaking of fire, darkness and weeping. In the parable of the sheep and goats he says that the wicked "will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46).

The Bible gives several descriptions: outer darkness, the lake of fire, the second death, the destruction of body and soul, separation from the presence of the Lord. Paul says that those who do not obey the gospel "will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might" (2 Thessalonians 1:9). It is described as just, and as the outcome of rejecting God's offer, never as the desire of God, who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11).

Christians have held three main views of its nature. The traditional view, held by most of the church through its history, is that hell is a state of conscious, unending punishment. The second, called annihilationism or conditional immortality, holds that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, and that the "eternal" refers to the result and not to the process. It has had thoughtful defenders among evangelicals, including Edward Fudge, and John Stott described it as a view he held tentatively. The third, universalism, holds that in the end all will be saved. A few early theologians, such as Origen, considered it, and some modern writers hold it, but the main body of the church has rejected it, in part because of the many warnings of Jesus.

Whatever the view, the doctrine is not meant to be held with relish. It makes the seriousness of sin plain, and it makes the cross more costly. And it is the reason Christians tell others the good news.

The one attribute the Bible repeats three times for emphasis is holiness. In Isaiah's vision of the temple, the seraphim cry to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory" (Isaiah 6:3). In Revelation the four living creatures say the same, day and night without rest. No other quality of God is raised to the third power in Scripture.

The root idea of holiness is separateness. God is set apart from creation, not in the sense of being far away, but in the sense of being utterly different. He is not simply the biggest and best of beings. He is of another order. Holiness also has a moral side. God is perfectly pure, without any trace of evil, and therefore he cannot approve of sin. These two meanings are joined: because God is wholly other, he is wholly good, and he is the standard for all goodness.

The right response is awe. When Isaiah sees the Lord, he does not say how wonderful it is. He says, "Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips" (Isaiah 6:5). The encounter with holiness reveals sin, and in the passage a seraph then touches his mouth with a coal from the altar and says his guilt is taken away. The same pattern runs through the Bible: holiness exposes, and mercy cleanses.

God does not keep his holiness to himself. He calls his people to share in it. Peter quotes from Leviticus: "just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do" (1 Peter 1:15). That is why the tabernacle and temple had boundaries and rules, why sin is serious, and why the cross was needed. Holiness is the reason the gospel is good news.
holy-holy-holy.q: When did you last feel something close to awe before God, and what produced it?

b: The Bible describes the effects of sin in several layers. The first is on our relationship with God. After the fall the man and woman hide from him, and Paul says that before Christ we were "dead in your trespasses and sins" (Ephesians 2:1). The second is on one another: blame, shame, violence and broken marriages come into the story at once. The third is on ourselves, in the form of a darkened mind, a hardened conscience, and desires that pull the wrong way. The fourth is on creation, which is "subjected to futility" and in "bondage to decay" until it is set free (Romans 8:20-21). And the fifth is death, which is the penalty for sin, and which enters through one man.

Theologians use the phrase total depravity, one of the points of the Reformed acronym TULIP. It is often misunderstood. It does not mean that people are as bad as they could be, or that they can do no good. Non-Christians can be kind, honest and brave. It means that sin has touched every part of a person, the mind, will, emotions and body, so that nothing in us is untouched, and that we are unable to save ourselves or to please God by our own power. The word "spiritually dead" describes the extent of the problem.

Not all Christians agree on how far inability goes. Reformed theology says that without the Spirit's work, a person cannot choose God, and that grace is irresistible. Arminians say that sin has made us unable to turn to God by ourselves, but that God gives a grace to everyone that frees the will enough to respond. Catholic theology teaches that human nature is wounded but not totally corrupted. The debate matters most for the doctrine of how people are saved.

The right response to this teaching is not to dwell on the dark side, but to see why the rescue was so costly. As Paul writes, "But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses" (Ephesians 2:4-5).

The New Testament says less about church government than people often expect, and Christians have organized the church in different ways. What it does show is that from the beginning local churches had leaders, and that qualifications of character mattered more than skills.

Two kinds of local office appear. The first are the overseers, also called elders or pastors. In Acts 20 Paul calls together "the elders of the church" at Ephesus and tells them that the Holy Spirit has made them "overseers" and that they are to "be shepherds of the church of God." Overseer (episkopos) and elder (presbyteros) seem to describe the same people from two angles (Titus 1:5-7). The second are deacons, who serve, and Acts 6 describes seven men appointed to care for the widows. The apostles had a unique role as eyewitnesses and founders.

Three main patterns have developed. The episcopal system is led by bishops, who oversee a region and who are held to stand in succession from the apostles. It is found in the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Methodist churches. The presbyterian system is led by elders, with local elders joined in regional courts, and it is found in the Presbyterian and Reformed churches. The congregational system holds that each local church governs itself under Christ, and it is found in Baptist, Congregational and many independent churches.

Each view appeals to the New Testament, and each has strengths. Early evidence is mixed. About AD 110, Ignatius of Antioch wrote of a single bishop in each city, with presbyters and deacons, while Clement of Rome a little earlier wrote as though the leaders in Corinth were the elders. Christians who disagree about government still share the main point: Christ is the head of the church, and its leaders are servants who will give an account.

Theologians distinguish two ways in which God reveals himself. The first is general revelation, which is available to everyone, everywhere, through creation and the human conscience. The second is special revelation, which comes through particular acts and words, in the history of Israel, in the Scriptures and above all in Jesus Christ.

The case for general revelation is made in a famous psalm: "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands. Day after day they pour forth speech" (Psalm 19:1-2). Paul adds that since the creation of the world God's "invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse" (Romans 1:20). The sky does not give a map to salvation, but it tells every person that there is a powerful and glorious Maker.

General revelation is real but not enough. It leaves people accountable without telling them how to be forgiven, and our fallen minds distort what we see. That is why God also spoke in particular ways. Hebrews opens with the claim that "On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son" (Hebrews 1:1-2). The Son is "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature."

Christians differ about how much can be known of God from nature apart from Scripture. Some traditions, including Roman Catholicism, hold that human reason can reach real truths about God by itself, such as his existence. Many Reformed thinkers hold that, because of sin, nature's testimony is truly clear but is not rightly received without God's grace. All agree that the fullest and clearest self-disclosure of God is the person of Jesus.

If Adam and Eve sinned in Genesis 3, how does that reach everyone else? The question is old, and the church has given more than one answer. The key text is Romans 5: "just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). Paul sets Adam against Christ: "just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19).

Augustine, the North African bishop who died in AD 430, taught that all humanity was somehow present in Adam, so that his sin is ours both in guilt and in a corrupt nature passed down. This is called original sin. He developed the view in his fight with Pelagius, a British monk who argued that people are born morally neutral and that Adam only set a bad example. The church at the Council of Carthage in AD 418 rejected Pelagius.

Later traditions refined the picture. Roman Catholics hold that original sin is inherited and removed by baptism, though it leaves a tendency toward sin. The Eastern Orthodox emphasize the inheritance of mortality and corruption more than of guilt. Lutheran and Reformed Christians stress that people are born guilty and corrupt. Some Protestants, including many Baptists and Wesleyans, hold that people inherit a corrupted nature and are accountable for their own sins. Many hold that children who die in infancy are saved by God's mercy.

All the major traditions agree that all people sin, that the tendency is present from the start (David says, "I was brought forth in iniquity," Psalm 51:5), and that the answer is found in Christ, the second Adam. The point of Romans 5 is not to puzzle us about Adam, but to say that if one man's act could bring so much ruin, one man's act of obedience can bring much more life.
Christians use several words to describe the quality of the Bible, and they do not all mean the same thing. Understanding the words helps in understanding the arguments.

Infallible means that Scripture will not fail or mislead us in what it teaches. Inerrant means that it is without error in all it affirms. Many Christians use the two words nearly interchangeably. Others prefer infallible, because inerrant seems to them to invite a demand for scientific precision that the text itself does not make. A group of evangelical scholars produced the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy in 1978, which says that Scripture is free from error in all its teaching, including matters of history and science when it speaks on them, while interpreting each passage according to its kind. Not every Christian tradition uses these words, but all the large traditions say that the Bible is trustworthy.

The question of what a passage actually affirms matters. Jesus' parables are not reports of events. Poetry uses imagery, and ancient writers described numbers and dates in conventions different from ours. The test is to ask what the author meant to say, and that requires attention to genre, which a later lesson takes up.

Two other claims are made. The first is clarity: the central message of the Bible is plain enough that an ordinary reader can understand how to be saved, even though some passages are hard (2 Peter 3:16). The second is sufficiency. Protestants hold that Scripture contains everything necessary for salvation and for the life of faith, and the psalm says that "The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree that Scripture is the supreme written authority but also hold that it was handed down within a church whose living tradition helps to interpret it.

Justification is the word the New Testament uses for the verdict of God on the believer. It is a courtroom word. To justify is to declare someone righteous, to acquit. Paul builds the main argument of Romans on it: "we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28), and "since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1).

The reason it needs saying is that every person stands guilty before God. No one can be declared righteous by keeping the law, since no one keeps it. Paul says in Galatians that "a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ." The ground of the verdict is not our own goodness but Christ's. In Romans 3 he says that people are "justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." Christ's righteousness is credited to those who trust him, as Abraham's faith "was credited to him as righteousness."

This was the center of the Reformation. Martin Luther said that this teaching is the article on which the church stands or falls. The Reformers said that justification is by faith alone, that it is a legal declaration, and that the righteousness is Christ's, given from outside us. The Catholic Church at the Council of Trent in 1547 replied that justification is not only a declaration but also an inner renewal, in which grace makes a person actually righteous, with faith working through love. For centuries this was a dividing line. In 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a Joint Declaration saying that the two sides now share a common understanding of the basics, while some differences of emphasis remain.

James says, "a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone" (James 2:24). Most Christians reconcile this with Paul by noting that James is talking about the kind of faith that is real, and that it shows itself in works. Paul and James both agree that the fruit of true faith is a changed life.

The Bible's answer to the question of what a human being is begins in Genesis 1: "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them" (Genesis 1:27). Nothing else in creation is said to be made in God's image. It is the thing that sets people apart from animals, and it is the basis of the dignity of every person.

What does the phrase mean? Christians have given three main answers, and most think the truth combines them. The structural view says the image is something in us, such as reason, conscience, moral awareness or the capacity to speak and love. The relational view says it is the ability to be in relationship with God and with each other, for God himself is a communion of persons. The functional view notes that the next sentence in Genesis speaks of ruling over creation, and says we image God by acting as his representatives, caring for the world on his behalf.

The consequences are far-reaching. Murder is wrong because the victim bears God's image (Genesis 9:6). Cursing a person is wrong because people "have been made in God’s likeness" (James 3:9). Every human life has value, whether it is useful or not, strong or weak, born or unborn, rich or poor. The Bible says that God made man "a little lower than the angels" and crowned him "with glory and honor" (Psalm 8:5).

The image was marred in the fall, but not erased, and the New Testament says it is being restored. Christ is "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), and those who belong to him are being "conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:29). The true human being is the one who shows us what the original design was meant to look like.
made-in-the-image-of-god.q: How would you treat people differently if you remembered all day that each one carries the image of God?

b: The first and greatest claim of the Bible about God is that there is only one. It was not self-evident in the ancient world. Egypt, Babylon and Canaan all had many gods: gods of the sun, the storm, the harvest and the sea. Israel alone, among its neighbors, confessed that the LORD is the only God, the creator of everything, and that there is none besides.

The great declaration is the Shema, spoken by Moses: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Isaiah gives the same message in God's own voice: "I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me" (Isaiah 45:5). Paul repeats it to the church in Corinth: "there is no God but one" (1 Corinthians 8:4). The Bible mocks idols, because they are made of wood and metal by people who need them.

This claim, called monotheism, has several consequences. If there is one God, then all of reality comes from one mind and one will, and there is a unity to truth. If there is one God, then there is one moral standard, and it is not a matter of what a tribe prefers. If there is one God, then he is the God of everyone, and no nation can claim him as its private possession. And if there is one God, then he alone deserves worship, and every other loyalty must be below it.

The New Testament holds this together with a remarkable additional claim: that this one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The doctrine of the Trinity, which a coming lesson takes up, does not abandon monotheism. It is the church's attempt to say who the one God has shown himself to be. Paul, a lifelong monotheist, can write that "for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ."
one-god-and-no-other.q: What difference does it make to your day to say that there is only one God?

b: The Trinity is the central and most distinctive teaching of Christianity about God. It says that there is one God, who eternally exists as three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The three are not three gods, and they are not three roles or masks that one person puts on. They are three who are distinct and yet share one divine nature.

The word does not appear in the Bible. It was used by Tertullian in North Africa around AD 200, and the doctrine was worked out because the Bible's data demanded it. The evidence has several parts. First, the Old and New Testaments insist that God is one. Second, the New Testament speaks of the Father as God, the Son as God, and the Holy Spirit as God. Third, the three appear together, as when Jesus tells his disciples to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), and when Paul closes a letter with a blessing from all three (2 Corinthians 13:14). Fourth, the three are distinguished from one another. The Son prays to the Father, the Father sends the Spirit, and at Jesus' baptism all three are present at once.

The church worked it out in the fourth century. At the Council of Nicaea in AD 325 it declared that the Son is "of one substance" with the Father, against Arius, who held that the Son was a created being. The Council of Constantinople in AD 381 affirmed the full deity of the Spirit and completed the Nicene Creed. The formula that emerged was one being, three persons.

No analogy is adequate. Water, ice and steam fail because they are one substance in three states, and a person who is father, son and husband fails because it is one person in three roles. The doctrine is held as a mystery that is revealed rather than explained. It also matters for what it says about God's character: before creation, God was already a communion of love, and love was never something he had to learn.

In the Old Testament three kinds of people were anointed with oil to serve God and his people: prophets, priests and kings. When the church tried to describe what Christ does, it noticed that he fulfills all three roles, and since John Calvin the pattern has been called the threefold office of Christ.

As prophet, Jesus speaks God's word to the people. Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like himself, whom the people must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15). Jesus teaches with authority, reveals the Father, and tells the future of the kingdom. Hebrews says that God, who spoke through the prophets, has spoken finally "by His Son."

As priest, Jesus represents the people before God. A priest offers sacrifice and prays. Jesus offered himself as the sacrifice, and he continues to intercede. Psalm 110 had spoken of a king who is also "a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek," and Hebrews takes the idea and shows that Jesus is this priest, with a priesthood that does not end because he lives forever.

As king, Jesus rules. He is the son of David who inherits the throne that was promised for ever. Zechariah had predicted that the king would come "righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9), and the Gospels show Jesus entering Jerusalem in that way. His kingdom is already present, in the church and in the hearts of those who follow him, and it will be complete when he returns.

The three offices answer three needs. We are ignorant, and the prophet teaches us. We are guilty, and the priest atones. We are weak and rebellious, and the king rules and protects. And they hold together in the one name, Christ, which means "the anointed one."

If creation is where the world starts, providence is how God keeps it going. The word, from the Latin for "foresight," names God's continuing care for and rule over everything he has made. The Bible does not picture a God who wound up the universe like a clock and then walked away.

Paul tells the Athenians that God "gives everyone life and breath and everything else" and that "in Him we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:25,28). Jesus says that God feeds the birds and clothes the lilies and that not one sparrow falls without the Father's knowledge. Hebrews says that Christ sustains "all things by His powerful word" (Hebrews 1:3). The psalm sees the rain, the grass, the wild animals and the harvest as all given by God's hand.

Theologians usually describe three parts to providence. Preservation means that God sustains the existence of creation. Concurrence means that God works through the actions of creatures, so that events have both natural and divine causes. Governance means that God directs everything toward his purposes. Together they mean that there is no corner of life outside God's care.

Providence is most comforting in trouble. "We know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose" (Romans 8:28). That does not mean that every event is good. It means that God is able to bring good out of it, as he did with Joseph in Egypt and with the cross.

Christians differ on the details, such as how God's providence relates to human freedom and to miracles, and on the hard question of evil. Some hold that God ordains everything, and others that he permits much that he does not will. But the heart of the doctrine is shared: the world has not been abandoned, and the one who made it looks after it.

The Bible says that God is in control of all things, and it says that people are responsible for what they choose. Both claims run through Scripture, often in the same passage. Peter says on the day of Pentecost that Jesus was handed over "by God’s set plan and foreknowledge," and that the people who did it acted by lawless hands (Acts 2:23). Joseph tells his brothers that although they meant evil, God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The proverb says, "A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).

Paul puts the two together in a single sentence: "continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose" (Philippians 2:12-13). He does not say that one is true and the other is only apparent. He says both, and he draws a practical conclusion from the pairing, which is humility and effort at once.

Christians have tried to explain how they fit together, and they have given different answers. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine and Calvin, stresses that God's rule is exhaustive and that his purposes cannot be thwarted, and it argues that human freedom is real but is exercised within God's decree. The Arminian and Wesleyan traditions stress that God has chosen to give people genuine freedom to respond, and that his foreknowledge does not remove it. Catholic and Orthodox traditions have their own versions of the question and emphasize both grace and cooperation.

All of them agree on some things. God is not the author of sin. People are not puppets. God's purposes will be accomplished. And the right response to God's rule is trust, and the right response to human duty is obedience. Most Christians have found that the mystery is easier to live in than to resolve.
sovereignty-and-human-responsibility.q: Where do you most struggle to hold both God's rule and your own responsibility?

b: Paul says that each believer is given something by the Holy Spirit to use for the good of the church: "There are different gifts, but the same Spirit," and "to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good" (1 Corinthians 12:4,7). Three of his letters contain lists: Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12 and Ephesians 4. They include teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy, administration, wisdom, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and their interpretation. The lists differ, so they appear to be illustrations and not a complete catalog.

Two principles stand out. The gifts are for others: they are given "for the common good" and not for personal display. And they require love. In the middle of the long discussion in 1 Corinthians comes chapter 13, which says that tongues, prophecy and knowledge are worth nothing without love, and chapter 14 then tells the church to pursue love and to seek gifts, "especially the gift of prophecy," which here means speech that builds the church up.

Christians have disagreed about whether all the gifts continue today. Cessationists hold that miraculous gifts such as prophecy, tongues and healing ceased with the apostolic age, once Scripture was complete. Continuationists hold that all the gifts continue and should be practiced with order. The modern Pentecostal movement began around 1901 in Topeka, Kansas, and the revival at Azusa Street in Los Angeles in 1906 spread it worldwide, and in the 1960s a charismatic renewal brought similar practices into older denominations. Today Pentecostals and charismatics number several hundred million. Many Christians fall somewhere between the two poles.
All agree that the church needs every part, as Paul says of the body: eye, hand and foot cannot say they have no need of one another.
spiritual-gifts.q: Which gift do you think you have been given, and who is it meant to serve?

b: When a person comes to faith, something happens that no one can bring about by willpower. Jesus tells Nicodemus: "Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again" (John 3:3). Nicodemus is puzzled, and Jesus explains that it is a birth "of water and the Spirit," and compares the Spirit to the wind: you hear it and see what it does, but you cannot control it.

Theologians call this regeneration. It is God's act of giving new spiritual life. Ezekiel had promised it centuries earlier: "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). Peter says that God "has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). Titus describes "the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit."

Before regeneration comes the call. The gospel is preached, and the Spirit works through it to draw people to Christ. Reformed theology distinguishes an outward call, which goes to everyone who hears, from an inward or effectual call, in which the Spirit makes the message take root. Arminian theology holds that the Spirit's grace goes to all and enables a response. Christians differ on the order, whether new birth comes before faith or after it, but they agree that both are the work of God.

The Bible also uses the image of rebirth in connection with baptism. Churches that practice infant baptism, such as the Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran, often link the two closely. Others hold that baptism is a sign of a new birth that has already happened. Whatever the view of the sign, the reality is that those who belong to Christ have been given a new life, and they are able to love what they once could not.

The most important question the New Testament asks is "Who is Jesus?" And its answer is bold: he is God the Son, who became a human being. The claim runs through the whole New Testament, and it was not invented by later councils.

John opens his Gospel with the plainest statement: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Then he says that "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). Paul writes that the Son "is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created." Everything was made through him, and "in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:15-17). The Gospels also say Jesus forgave sins, which only God can do, accepted worship, and said "before Abraham was born, I am" (John 8:58), taking the divine name from Exodus 3.

In a famous hymn Paul writes that Christ Jesus, "existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7). The Greek verb for "emptied" does not mean that he gave up being God. It means that he took the lowest possible position while remaining who he was.

Early in church history some taught that Jesus was a created being, or that he was a man adopted by God, or that he only seemed to be human. The Council of Nicaea in AD 325 rejected the view of Arius, who said "there was a time when he was not," and confessed that the Son is "God from God, light from light, true God from true God." The Christian claim is not that Jesus was an unusually good man or a great teacher. It is that the one who made the world walked in it.

When Jesus taught his disciples to pray, he began with a word that startled his hearers: "Our Father in heaven." The Old Testament uses the image of father for God a handful of times. In the Gospels it is the name Jesus uses almost every time he speaks of God, and in Aramaic he addressed God as Abba, the word a child used for a father at home.

The Father is the first person of the Trinity, and the Bible associates him with certain acts in particular. He is the source: "from Him and through Him and to Him are all things." He is the planner, and the plan of salvation begins in his choice: "He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:4-5). He sends the Son, and he gives the Spirit. Everything flows from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and it returns to the Father in praise.

The title Father tells us what God is like in relation to his people. A father provides, protects, disciplines and delights in his children. Paul says that those who belong to Christ received "the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (Romans 8:15). The same Spirit testifies that we are God's children.

Christians have also stressed that God the Father is not male in the way humans are. The Bible uses images of motherhood for God occasionally (Isaiah 66:13), and it denies that God has a body (John 4:24). The name Father is the one that Jesus gave, and so the church has kept it. Jesus also said that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9), so what we learn about the Father, we learn by looking at the Son.

The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, and the one that is hardest to picture. The Bible uses images such as wind, breath, fire, water and a dove, and these tell us about what the Spirit does, but not about who he is. It is important to see that the Bible speaks of the Spirit as a person and not just as a force or influence.

The evidence is in how he is described. He teaches, speaks, testifies, guides, intercedes, and can be grieved or lied to (Ephesians 4:30; Acts 5:3). Jesus calls him "another Advocate," a word meaning someone who comes alongside, and says he will be with the disciples forever: "the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you" (John 14:16-17). Peter tells Ananias that lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3-4), which places the Spirit with God.

The Spirit has been active since the first verses of Genesis, where he hovers over the waters. In the Old Testament he empowers leaders, artists and prophets. After Pentecost, he comes to live in all believers. His work includes convicting the world of sin, giving new birth, opening the Scriptures, producing the fruit of love, joy and peace, giving gifts for service, and assuring believers that they are God's children. "the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words" when we do not know how to pray (Romans 8:26).

Jesus says that the Spirit "will not speak on His own," but will take what is Christ's and declare it to us (John 16:13-14). So the Spirit's work always points to the Son. A Christian is someone in whom the Spirit has begun to make Christ real, and the whole of life, from first faith to final resurrection, is lived in his power.

The Bible says that history will end with a judgment. This is part of its good news as well as its warning. A world in which evil never faced consequences, in which the powerful oppressed the weak and died in their beds, would not be a just world. The judgment is God's promise to put things right.

The judge is Jesus. Paul says to the Athenians that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world by a man he appointed, and gave proof by raising him from the dead. Jesus himself says that "When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne. All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats" (Matthew 25:31-32). The scene in Revelation 20 shows a great white throne and the dead standing before it, with books opened.

The basis is our deeds, as evidence of the heart. "We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad" (2 Corinthians 5:10). Believers are not judged for salvation, since Christ has borne that, but they do give an account of their lives, and Paul says that there will be rewards, and that some work will be burned up (1 Corinthians 3:13-15). Those who are not in Christ are judged by what they have done and by what they have done with what they knew.

The truth of the judgment is meant to produce seriousness and hope. It tells us that nothing is hidden and that every wrong will be addressed, and also that mercy is available now. The same Jesus who will be the judge is the one who offers forgiveness today.

On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and a cup, shared them with his disciples and told them to repeat it in his memory. Paul passes on the account: "The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, 'This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.'" And after supper the cup: "This cup is the new covenant in My blood" (1 Corinthians 11:23-25). The church has kept this meal ever since, and it is called by several names: the Lord's Supper, Communion, the Eucharist (from the Greek for thanksgiving) and the Mass.

The meaning is rich. It looks back, since it is a memorial of the cross. It looks inward, to a participation in Christ, since Paul asks, "Is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?" It looks around, because "we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf" (1 Corinthians 10:17). And it looks forward, because Paul says that each time we eat and drink, "you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes."

The disagreement is about how Christ is present. The Catholic Church teaches transubstantiation, that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ while their appearances remain, a doctrine given its name in the twelfth century and defined at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215. The Orthodox churches hold that Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a mystery. Martin Luther taught that Christ's body and blood are present "in, with and under" the bread and wine, which is sometimes called sacramental union. John Calvin taught that Christ is truly present by the Holy Spirit, who lifts believers to feed on him spiritually. Huldrych Zwingli, and later many Baptists and others, taught that the meal is a memorial and a sign. Luther and Zwingli met at Marburg in 1529 and could not agree on this one point.
Paul warns believers to examine themselves before taking part. Whatever one's view, the meal says that Christians live by Christ's sacrifice and not by their own.

The church exists for a purpose beyond itself. Jesus said, in his last words to the disciples, "Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:19-20). This is called the Great Commission, and it has driven the church's mission across two thousand years.

The commission has several parts. It is to go, and to make disciples, which means more than getting decisions; a disciple is a follower who learns. It is to baptize, which brings people into the community. And it is to teach obedience, which means that conversion is a start and not an end. The scope is "all nations," so that no group of people is outside its reach. Acts 1:8 draws the map: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

Paul gives another way of describing it. God "reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation," and so believers are "ambassadors for Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:18-20). Jesus also says that his followers are "the salt of the earth" and "the light of the world" (Matthew 5:13-14), which means that the church serves society by being what it is, and by doing good works that give glory to the Father.

Christians have held that mission includes both word and deed: preaching the gospel and caring for the poor, the sick and the oppressed, as Jesus did. The balance has been argued at different times. Through history, the church has founded hospitals, schools and universities, and it has sent missionaries. Today most Christians live outside Europe and North America. The commission is still unfinished, and it still carries Jesus' promise that he is with them.

The creeds confess "the resurrection of the body," and the claim is more specific than a general belief in life after death. It says that God will raise the dead and give them new bodies, and that the final hope is not the soul's escape from the body, but the redemption of the whole person.

The Old Testament hints at it. Daniel 12:2 says, "Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt." Job says that after his skin has been destroyed, yet from his flesh he will see God (Job 19:26). The New Testament pushes it into the open with the resurrection of Jesus, which is the pattern and the guarantee. Paul argues in 1 Corinthians 15 that Christ is the firstfruits, and that "in Christ all will be made alive."

What kind of body will it be? Paul compares it to a seed. What is put in the ground is not what comes up. The body is "sown perishable" and "raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). A spiritual body does not mean a ghost. It means a body suited to the Spirit, with continuity and transformation, like the body of the risen Jesus, who could be touched and who also passed through locked doors.

Jesus says that all will be raised: "all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment" (John 5:28-29). The resurrection of believers is the climax of salvation, and it gives dignity to the body now. Christians have always treated the bodies of the dead with respect and have resisted views that despise the body. What is sown in tears will be raised in glory.

The New Testament says repeatedly that Jesus will come back. When he ascended, two men in white told the watching disciples, "This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11). This is the second coming, and the early church lived in expectation of it. The earliest Christian prayer we know was an Aramaic phrase, Maranatha, "Our Lord, come."

The return will be personal and visible. It will not be a spiritual impression or the spread of Christian ideas. Jesus says that "the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven" and "all the tribes of the earth will mourn" (Matthew 24:30). Paul describes it for the church at Thessalonica: "the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise" (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

The timing is not given. Jesus is plain: "No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Matthew 24:36). Throughout history, many people have predicted a date, and each time they have been wrong, which Jesus' words would predict. He says instead that his people should be watchful and faithful, like servants who do not know when the master will be back.

The return has several purposes. It will complete salvation, for the dead will be raised and the living changed. It will bring judgment, for he will judge the living and the dead. It will defeat all evil, and it will begin the new creation. Paul says that believers await "the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" (Titus 2:13). The hope is not meant to make Christians idle or fearful. It makes them hopeful and ready.

All four Gospels present Jesus as someone without sin. He is tempted, but he does not fall. He is accused of many things, but when he challenges his opponents with "Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?" (John 8:46), no one answers. Those who knew him best bear the same witness. Peter says that "He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth" (1 Peter 2:22). Paul says that God made "Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Hebrews adds that we have a high priest who "was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin" (Hebrews 4:15).

The sinlessness of Jesus has two uses. It qualifies him to be the sacrifice for sin. In the Old Testament a lamb offered for sin had to be without blemish, and a person who is himself guilty cannot make up for another's guilt. Jesus' perfect life is what makes his death a worthy offering. And it gives him a perfect obedience that can be credited to others. Paul says that "through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19), and Reformed theology calls this the active obedience of Christ.

It also matters for how we think of temptation. Jesus' temptation in the wilderness was real, and he resisted it by trusting God's word. Because he faced temptation without giving in, he understands it more fully than we do, since the person who never yields feels the full force of the pressure. Hebrews tells believers to "approach the throne of grace with confidence," because we are not coming to a judge who cannot sympathize. We are coming to one who has been where we are.
the-sinless-life-of-jesus.q: What would it mean to you that Jesus faced every kind of temptation and never gave in?

b: Revelation 20 speaks of a period of a thousand years, in which Satan is bound and the saints reign with Christ. The passage has been read in three main ways, and the labels come from how each connects the return of Christ with the thousand years.

Amillennialism takes the thousand years as a symbolic description of the present age, between Christ's first and second coming, during which Satan's power has been limited and believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven. Christ's return will bring the end of history, the resurrection and the final judgment. It was the view of Augustine, and it is the view of the Catholic and Orthodox churches and of many Reformed and Lutheran Christians.

Postmillennialism holds that the gospel will spread and bring a long period of peace and righteousness on the earth, after which Christ will return. It was widely held among Puritans and by Jonathan Edwards, and it was popular in the nineteenth century, but it lost ground after the two world wars of the twentieth century.

Premillennialism holds that Christ will return before a literal thousand years of his reign on earth. Some of the early Christians, such as Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, held something like this, and it is called historic premillennialism. A later form, called dispensationalism, was developed by John Nelson Darby in the nineteenth century and spread through the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909. It divides history into distinct ages, sees a future role for national Israel, and often teaches a rapture of the church before a period of tribulation.

Within these views Christians also differ about the timing of the tribulation and the rapture, which Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 as believers being "caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air." None of this is part of the historic creeds. The creeds confess only that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

The word incarnation comes from Latin and means "becoming flesh." It names the central event of Christian history: that God the Son took on a full human nature and was born as a baby in Bethlehem. John says it in one line: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14).

Several things stand out in the New Testament accounts. First, the birth was a real birth. The Son was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of Mary, a virgin, and grew like any child. He was hungry, tired and thirsty. He grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52). He wept at the grave of Lazarus. He suffered and died. Second, he took our nature for a purpose.
