Hebrews says, "Since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14). He had to become like his brothers in every way, in order to be a merciful and faithful high priest.

Third, he did not stop being God. Paul says that he "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7). The best understanding has been that he laid aside the privileges of divine glory, but not his divine nature. The one who made the world became a creature, and he did so without losing anything of what he is.

The incarnation is God's answer to the question of how a holy God can be close to sinful people. He did not shout across a distance. He came. It is the reason Christians say that Jesus reveals God, and the reason the church has insisted so firmly on both halves of the claim, that he is truly God and truly man, and that if either is lost, the gospel is lost.

Once the church affirmed that Jesus is God and that he is man, the next question was how the two fit together. The fifth century was spent on it, and the answer remains the standard for almost all Christians: Jesus is one person with two natures, divine and human.

Several wrong turns were taken and rejected. Docetism held that Jesus only seemed to have a body. Arianism held that he was a created being. Apollinarianism held that he had a human body but not a human mind. Nestorianism seemed to divide him into two persons, one divine and one human. Eutychianism, or monophysitism, held that the two natures were blended into one, so that his humanity was swallowed up. Each of these tries to simplify the mystery by dropping one half of the truth.

The Council of Chalcedon met in AD 451 near Constantinople and issued a definition that is still honored by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches. It confesses one and the same Christ, the Son, the Lord, "in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation." The differences of the natures are not removed by their union, and the properties of each are preserved in one person. The Oriental Orthodox churches, such as the Coptic and Armenian, did not accept the council, but today many of them hold that the disagreement was largely about words.

This means that what Jesus did, he did as one person. When he was hungry, it was the Son of God who was hungry. When he said to the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven, it was a man who spoke with God's authority. Paul says, "For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9). Because he is truly man he can represent us, and because he is truly God his sacrifice can save.

If you read the letters of Paul looking for a phrase that sums up his view of the Christian life, you might choose "in Christ." It appears in some form well over a hundred times. Many theologians, including Calvin, have argued that union with Christ is the master idea behind salvation: not a separate step along with justification and sanctification, but the reality that holds them all together.

The Bible speaks of this union in many pictures. Jesus says, "I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit" (John 15:5). Paul speaks of the church as the body of Christ, with Christ as the head. He speaks of a marriage between Christ and the church. He says believers are in Christ and Christ is in them, and that the Holy Spirit is the bond.

Union means that what happened to Christ is counted as having happened to us. Paul says, "all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death. We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:3-4). To be united with Christ is to die with him to sin and rise with him to a new life. In Galatians Paul says, "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me."

The doctrine also explains why believers receive every benefit of salvation together. Forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the hope of resurrection and the promise of glory all come with Christ, since he cannot be divided. The Orthodox tradition speaks of theosis, becoming partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), and means something similar. Whatever the vocabulary, the heart of the Christian life is not a set of rules, but a person, and a relationship with him.

Theologians sort the qualities of God into two groups, and the sorting is helpful even though it is a human tool. The first group are the incommunicable attributes, those that belong to God alone and that no creature shares. The second are the communicable attributes, which God has in perfect form and which we can reflect in limited ways, since we are made in his image.
Among the first group are these.

- Independence, or aseity: God needs nothing and depends on nothing. He is the source of everything else.
- Eternity: God has no beginning or end and is not bound by time as we are.
- Immutability: God does not change in his character, his purposes or his promises.
- Omnipresence: God is present everywhere. "Where can I go to escape Your Spirit?" asks the psalmist (Psalm 139:7).
- Omniscience: God knows everything, past, present and future.
- Omnipotence: God can do all that is consistent with his nature, which means that he cannot lie or deny himself.

The communicable attributes include holiness, love, goodness, justice, mercy, wisdom, faithfulness and patience. A few verses carry many of them at once. When God passed in front of Moses on Sinai, he said that he is "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The prophet Jeremiah says that the LORD is "the true God; He is the living God and eternal King" (Jeremiah 10:10).

None of these is a separate piece. God is not partly love and partly justice. Each attribute describes the whole of God from a different angle, and each is perfectly harmonious with the others. The Bible does not give us a list of properties. It shows us a person, in his dealings with creation and with his people, and the doctrine of God is just that person's biography put into careful words.

Sin is the central problem in the Bible, and the Bible has more than one word for it. The most common Hebrew and Greek words describe missing a mark, going astray, crossing a line, rebellion, guilt and uncleanness. Together they paint sin as many things: a failure to hit the target, a path that wanders off, a wall that is crossed, a debt that is owed, a stain that needs cleaning.

At its heart, sin is a failure to love and honor God as he deserves. John writes, "Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness" (1 John 3:4). Paul says that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). When David confesses his adultery and murder, he says to God, "Against You, You only, have I sinned" (Psalm 51:4), because every wrong done to another person is also a wrong against the Lord of all.

Sin includes actions, but it is not limited to them. Jesus taught that anger is a root of murder and lust of adultery. Sin includes attitudes, words and omissions. James says, "Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin" (James 4:17). Sin also includes a condition, a bent in the human heart, so that people sin because they are sinners and not only the reverse.

Because sin offends against a holy God, it is serious. It cannot be dealt with by saying that it does not matter, or by doing more good deeds than bad, since a debt is not paid by earning other money. The Bible's answer is that sin has to be forgiven and removed, and that only God can do that. The doctrine of sin is not meant to leave us in despair, but to show the need for the doctrine of salvation, and the whole of the gospel depends on taking the first seriously.
what-sin-is.q: Which kind of sin is easiest for you to excuse: the sin of doing wrong or the sin of leaving good undone?

b: The English word church translates the Greek ekklesia, which in ordinary use meant an assembly of citizens called together. The Old Testament Greek used it for Israel gathered before God, and the New Testament takes it for the community of people who belong to Jesus. Jesus himself uses the word only twice in the Gospels, and one of those is the promise, "I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18).

The church is not a building. It is a people. Peter calls it "a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light" (1 Peter 2:9). The New Testament gives it many images: a body with Christ as head, a flock with a shepherd, a family, a temple built of living stones, a bride waiting for her husband, an army, a field and a vine. Each of them stresses that belonging to Christ means belonging to others.

Christians distinguish the universal church, which is all believers in every place and time, from the local church, which is a particular gathering in a place. The Nicene Creed confesses that the church is "one, holy, catholic and apostolic": one, because Christ has one body; holy, because it is set apart by God; catholic, which means universal; and apostolic, because it rests on the apostles' teaching. The Reformers added that the marks of a true church are the right preaching of the word and the right administration of the sacraments, and Calvin added discipline.

The early church, according to Acts, "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer" (Acts 2:42). Those four activities, teaching, community, the Lord's Supper and prayer, remain the core of church life. The Bible has no picture of a Christian living in isolation, and Hebrews tells believers not to neglect meeting together.
what-the-church-is.q: What is one way you depend on other Christians that you would not manage alone?

b: The cross is the center of the Christian faith, and the New Testament describes what happened there in many ways. The church has never officially adopted a single theory of the atonement, a word meaning "at-one-ment," the reconciling of God and humanity. It has gathered several biblical pictures, each of which captures part of the truth.

Ransom. Jesus said that he came "to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). A ransom is a price paid to free someone held captive. Early Christian writers such as Origen and Gregory of Nyssa built on this picture, and some of them asked whom the price was paid to.

Victory. Paul says that on the cross God "disarmed the powers and authorities" and made a public spectacle of them, "triumphing over them by the cross" (Colossians 2:15). The Swedish theologian Gustaf Aulén called this view Christus Victor in 1931, and the Eastern church has long stressed it.

Satisfaction and substitution. Paul says that God presented Jesus "as an atoning sacrifice in His blood" to demonstrate his righteousness (Romans 3:25). Anselm of Canterbury, in 1098, argued that the offense against God's honor required satisfaction. The Reformers, notably Calvin, added that Christ took the penalty of sin in our place. Peter says, "He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree" (1 Peter 2:24). This view is called penal substitution, and many evangelicals hold it as central.

Example and love. Peter says Christ left us an example. In the twelfth century Peter Abelard argued that the cross shows us God's love so that it moves us to love him in return, which is called the moral influence view.

Many theologians say that each of these has strong biblical support, and that the weakest accounts are the ones that choose one and throw out the rest. All of them agree on the main thing. The death of Jesus was not an accident or a defeat. It was the purposeful act by which God dealt with sin, defeated evil and reconciled the world to himself.

Theology means, literally, words about God. It is the work of thinking carefully and honestly about who God is and what he has done, and it is as old as the Bible itself. Everyone has a theology. A person who says that God is whatever you want him to be is doing theology, and so is one who says there is no God at all. The question is not whether to have one but whether it is well founded.

Christians usually divide the subject into branches. Biblical theology follows the story and the themes of the Bible as they unfold. Systematic theology gathers what the Bible teaches on a topic, such as God or salvation, and arranges it into an orderly whole. Historical theology studies how the church has understood these things over the centuries. Practical theology asks how it should shape worship, preaching and daily life.

The sources are ranked. Scripture is the final authority for most Christians, and Protestants say it alone is the norm that judges all others. The church's tradition is a trusted guide to how Scripture has been read, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians give it more weight than Protestants do. Reason is needed to read well and to draw conclusions. Experience can confirm or challenge our reading but cannot overrule the text.

Theology is not meant to be mere information. Jesus says, "this is eternal life: that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). The aim is to know a person, and the study succeeds when it ends in worship and obedience. Paul says Scripture is given so that the believer may be "complete, fully equipped for every good work."
what-theology-is-for.q: What is one belief about God that you hold only because someone told you, and what would it take to test it against Scripture?

b: Worship is the response of a creature to the glory of God, and it is what the church exists to do. Jesus told the woman at the well that the Father is looking for people who "will worship the Father in spirit and in truth" (John 4:23-24), which means that the place matters less than the heart and the truth about God.

The earliest Christians were Jews, who worshiped in the temple and synagogue, and they took over many of its elements: reading Scripture, singing psalms, prayer and teaching. They added the breaking of bread and the confession that Jesus is Lord. By about AD 150, Justin Martyr described a Sunday meeting in which the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets were read, the leader preached, the people prayed, bread and wine were shared, and a collection was taken for the poor. The outline is close to what most churches do today.

Christians met on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection. Acts says, "On the first day of the week we came together to break bread" (Acts 20:7), and Paul tells the Corinthians to set aside a gift on the first day of each week. John calls it "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10). Over time this replaced the Sabbath for most Christians, and in AD 321 the emperor Constantine made Sunday a day of rest in the empire.

Christians differ about whether the fourth commandment, the Sabbath, still applies on Sunday. Some, such as the Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday. Many Reformed Christians hold that the Sabbath principle carries over to Sunday. Others see Sunday as a day of worship that does not carry the same rest requirements, and hold that Christ is the believer's rest (Hebrews 4). Churches also differ in style, from the stately liturgy of Orthodox and Anglican services to the freedom of Quaker silence or Pentecostal exuberance. What is common is the center: the word, prayer, praise and the table, gathered around Christ.
